articles.title: Is the US blue wave a turning point for Europe, too?
articles.summary: Far right populists remain insurgent and pro-EU governments are braced for a lame duck Trump’s betrayal. But the mid-terms also showed that democracy can fight back
body: “Is Maga dead?” asked Margaret, a Guardian reader in Switzerland, in a live Q&A with our correspondents after the seismic US midterm elections. If Margaret’s query expressed a hope that the Democrats’ blue wave could transform Europe’s fortunes after two years of Maga-induced trauma, she was probably not alone.

The resounding defeat for Donald Trump’s Republicans and the installation of a Democratic-controlled US Congress has been met with understandable relief in European capitals. In the short term however, the worst for Europe is not over. Trump didn’t need congressional approval, after all, to unleash a trade war on his supposed European allies, threaten to invade Greenland, try to stitch up Ukraine or go to war with Iran, an act that has inflated fuel and food prices disastrously.

Hemmed in now on domestic policy, the US president may, many European leaders fear, use his extensive foreign policy powers to become even more confrontational on the world stage. Europe, warned Nathalie Tocci, is exactly where Trump will lash out. “Trump and Maga have always seen Europe as the mirror image of their domestic foes: a bunch of presumptuous, woke, emasculated liberals. Now that those foes have made a comeback at home, Trump’s rancour towards Europe is likely to grow.”

The lashing out could come in the form of new tariff chaos. As the humiliated Maga figurehead (one Washington expert likened the movement now to “a cornered ferret”), Trump could veto aid for Ukraine and thwart Kyiv’s access to defence technology. Paul Taylor sketched a fearful scenario in which he could even attempt a carve-up of eastern Europe in the so-called “big, beautiful deal” for Ukraine that he says he is working on with Russia. The omens for Europe were poor as US-mediated talks opened in Abu Dhabi, with delegates from Germany, France, the UK and the EU, literally sidelined.

Nor can Europe rely on the new intake of congressional Democrats to challenge Trump on its behalf, Blanche Leridon of the Institut Montaigne thinktank in Paris, tells me. “We have to be clear-sighted that the Democrats’ priority in Congress won’t be to re-establish a more harmonious relationship with Europe. Their foreign policy is, at this point, difficult to decipher. There isn’t a single, consistent position between the more progressive and centrist factions when it comes to either Europe or Ukraine specifically.”

We can’t even assume that nationalist populist parties, encouraged by Trump to destroy the EU from the inside, will suffer by their association with him. True, in central and eastern Europe, where the Maga spirit was heavily promoted by Viktor Orbán, some incumbents may have to perform a pivot. Poland’s conservative president Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by the opposition Eurosceptic Law and Justice party and has vaunted his proximity to Trump, is now facing awkward questions. And in Czechia, which has one of the most pro-Maga governments in Europe, populist PM Andrej Babiš and his far-right coalition partners, the Motorists party, have faced a wave of grassroots protests lately.
In Italy meanwhile, the far-right prime minister Giorgia Meloni played up tensions with Trump months ago, a strategic move to allay the concerns of voters, the majority of whom despise him.

But in countries where populists have not yet been in government and are polling at record levels, Trump’s humiliation may not matter to voters, even if their grievances – such as stagnant pay, inflation and lack of affordable housing – are often driven by global forces.

“It would be wrong to conclude that national-populist and reactionary forces are in retreat everywhere in the west,” Leridon says. “The Democrats won in the US because people were fed up with Trump, in Serbia, [Aleksandar] Vučić was overthrown after 14 years, but in countries where populist political forces are not in power, but on the verge of gaining it, the calculation is different.”

In France, Marine Le Pen is still leading in the polls, six months ahead of a presidential election being fought on cost-of-living issues. Her far-right National Rally party identified Trump as a liability some time ago. “Le Pen and [Jordan] Bardella understood perfectly the radioactive effect the US president could have on them as politicians claiming to defend French national interests. Above all, they recoiled from the corrosive impact of Trump’s policies on purchasing power in France, whether via trade tariffs or the war in Iran,” Leridon says.

In Germany, Alice Weidel, a co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, had also distanced the party from Trump in response to tariffs and Greenland. Weidel now blames Trump’s defeat on broken promises about going to war with Iran.

A critical test for Europe’s political direction is looming in Spain. Socialist prime minister Pedro Sánchez, who called a snap election for 29 November, welcomed Trump’s defeat as a straw in the wind for the revival of progressive forces. But amid public outcry over housing and wages (the cause of Wednesday’s general strike), the momentum is with the opposition rightwing Popular Party (PP) – which could coalesce with the far-right Vox. If this happens, it will be the first time a far-right party enters government in Spain since the end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975. Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, dismissed any suggestion of an ideological connection with Trump’s Republicans. “We are in Spain, not in Michigan,” he said after the midterms.
A yearning for generational change

And yet, longer term, the broader, more hopeful lesson from across the Atlantic could be that after years of global backsliding liberal democracy is not dead. “If Europe can celebrate an essential point, it is that American democracy is alive and was the big winner of these elections,” Leridon says.

Could this even, as Alexander Hurst asked, be a “democratic spring” – one that began in Budapest in April with Orbán’s defeat? Julian Borger unpacked how a sequence of four pivotal elections this year, in Hungary, Serbia, Brazil and now the US, has shown the power of grassroots activism to produce surprises and could, perhaps, begin the reversal of a worldwide drift towards authoritarianism.

The US vote could even shake Europe’s ailing mainstream parties out of their fatalistic mimicking of far-right policies and into action. Gen Z voters fuelled the US blue wave, which showed a yearning for generational change. At a time when youth-led protest movements have rocked Europe, progressive parties may be able to channel protest energy into serious political change. They can’t say they haven’t been warned, loudly, to heed calls for democratic renewal, education, decent housing, equality and limits on the power of the big tech billionaires. Or that failure to do so could allow grassroots anger to be co-opted into the same kind of anti-system nihilism that fuelled Maga.

articles.title: ‘Hear the goals during the afterlife’: Barça fans get to inter ashes at club’s new memorial
articles.summary: Memorial FC Barcelona, part of upgrade to Camp Nou stadium, will consist of 26,000 niches where fans can deposit their ashes
body: Lifelong supporters of Barcelona football club will soon be able to cheer on the club from beyond the grave – but, like everything else at Barça, eternal devotion comes at a price.
As part of an upgrade to the Camp Nou, the club has inaugurated the Memorial FC Barcelona, consisting of 26,000 niches where fans can deposit their ashes after their own final whistle has blown.

Supporting the team from the afterlife will cost €2,490 (£2,082) for 10 years or €6,000 for 50 years, with an annual maintenance fee of €70. Guaranteeing your niche for eternity will set you back €10,000, with a further €490 for a memorial plaque.
Related: Don’t call it a remontada: Emery’s Camp Nou comeback focuses European blur

Presenting the Memorial FC Barcelona, María Elena Fort, the club’s institutional vice-president, said: “When my grandfather died many years ago, he said the only thing he wanted was to be buried next to Barça’s pitch so that he could hear the goals go in during the afterlife. Many fans dream of the same thing.”

The memorial, designed by the architect Quique Montoya, will consist of four large illuminated squares, while the memorial plaques will be installed in a glass wall backlit with LED lights. The urns will be kept behind a mural commemorating key moments in the club’s 125-year history.
The rival Spanish clubs Atlético Madrid, Betis and Espanyol already have smaller columbariums in their stadiums.

Work on Barcelona’s will begin late next year and the club says more than 1,000 Barça fans have already booked their place. Their contributions will go towards paying the huge cost of redeveloping the stadium, which was built in 1957.

In 2023, the club embarked on a scheme to increase capacity from 99,354 to 105,000 – 15,000 more than Wembley Stadium and making it the second biggest football venue in the world, after the Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in Pyongyang in North Korea.
The cost of the changes, initially costed at €900m, is now approaching €2bn, now being borne by non-season ticket holders who have seen ticket prices double in recent years.

The work, being carried out by the Turkish firm Limak Construction, has been plagued by delays and labour disputes. In 2024, FC Barcelona recognised that, among other abuses, more than 1,000 subcontractors had not been paid for overtime.
Work is due to be completed later this year but the club will have to play part of next season at the Olympic Stadium (capacity 55,926) while a roof is installed on Camp Nou.

articles.title: Killing of journalist underscores deteriorating conditions in Ecuador
articles.summary: Tomás Beltrán was shot dead amid gang warfare that has turned Latin American country into one of its most violent
body: Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.

Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.

Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.

Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.
Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.

“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.

“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.

The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub, particularly through the Pacific.
Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.

“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.
“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.

Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.

While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated, a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.

There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.
Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.
“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”

articles.title: Millions join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years in protest at rising housing costs
articles.summary: The 24-hour stoppage has drawn high participation across sectors and comes weeks before election in which far right could gain power
body: Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
At the centre of Wednesday’s nationwide 24-hour stoppage, singularly backed by the country’s largest unions as well as tenants’ associations, is a pushback against Spain’s deepening housing crisis.

Sandra Mora, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told the broadcaster RNE: “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers – who are also renters or who also pay mortgages – are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill.”

While workers’ unions reported high participation in the strike across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, they said participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions, such as Catalonia and Andalusia, where the soaring cost of housing has been particularly acute.

Many schools and universities were reportedly closed or working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, the labour action added to an ongoing strike by teachers that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.

In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks – some with burning tyres – as public transport came to a near-standstill. In Madrid, scuffles broke out between picketers and police near the country’s main wholesale market, while demonstrators dragged ⁠large recycling bins on to the streets to block traffic. By midday on Wednesday, government officials said 27 people had been arrested over minor incidents across the country.

Stormy weather loomed over the plans for afternoon marches across the country after Spain’s state meteorological agency issued 14 alerts for two storms that were expected to bring strong winds, rough seas and heavy rains.

The long-simmering frustration at soaring housing prices across Spain burst into public view in September after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the home in which she had lived for more than seven decades.

As protests and encampments sprang up across Spain, it cast a spotlight on a market where properties were increasingly being used as tourist lets, speculative assets and short-term rentals, sending rents rising by 80% within a decade while the cost of homes climbed by 63%.

Before Wednesday’s strike, the tenants’ union of Granada sought to highlight this link, descending on the city’s most touristed areas to vandalise about 300 lockboxes belonging to short-term rentals. “No to capitalists, no to rent-seekers, no to their accomplices,” the organisation wrote on social media, as they posted pictures of lockboxes that had been rendered unusable.

Housing campaigners and unions have called on the government to do more to intervene in the market, with tenants’ unions demanding measures such as limits on the evictions of vulnerable people, rent freezes and a crackdown on short-term rentals.
Unai Sordo, the head of one of the country’s biggest labour unions, the Workers’ Commissions, told Cadena Ser radio: “There is one issue that is dividing the country: the struggle to access housing.”

Spain is holding a general election on 29 November. The snap vote was called by the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis.
Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.

While Sánchez has sought to focus the campaign on social issues, the discussion has shifted to questions over infrastructure after at least 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year.

This week Sánchez seized on the strike, whose official slogan is “Salaries. Housing. Prices”, as a way to recast the spotlight, posting a video in which he lauded developments such as the eight-hour workday and national health insurance and credited them to the labour movement and the right to strike. “It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said.
His position sharply contrasted with the discourse of parties on the right who, in the lead-up to the strike, said unions were trying to help Sánchez remain in office.

This week the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, accused striking workers of “holding citizens hostage”. Ayuso, who this year faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office, added: “Everything is chaotic, everything is gridlocked.”

While she acknowledged that union activity is a constitutional right, she also said she had vented her frustrations to the leader of the People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who polls suggest will be the next prime minister. “I’ll confess something,” she told Spanish television. “I spoke to Feijóo and I told him: ‘Promise me this garbage will end.’”

articles.title: Belgian plan for ICE-style immigration raids on homes criticised as ‘law of fear’
articles.summary: Rights groups oppose law that will let police forcibly enter homes to remove refused asylum seekers
body: Belgium could see ICE-style home raids that echo the US crackdown on immigration, rights campaigners have warned, after MPs approved a law that allows police to forcibly enter properties to remove undocumented people.

For months, intense debate has swirled across Belgium over measures introduced by the ruling right-leaning coalition to ramp up expulsions of people who have been denied the right to stay in the country.

In the run-up to the parliamentary vote last Friday, more than 60 protests were held across the country, adding to criticism voiced by NGOs, judges and lawyers’ associations over the measures. Some have drawn parallels with the US, where arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement have soared under Donald Trump’s administration.

The law, which is set to take effect next spring, gives the Belgian immigration office the power to ask an investigating judge to authorise entry into residences that may be housing anyone without papers, including homes where migrants are being hosted by friends or family.

Once this warrant has been obtained, police will be able to enter people’s homes without consent between 5am and 9pm, potentially in the presence of children. Once inside, they can detain people and carry out searches for identity documents.

“It’s a law of fear,” said Carine Thibaut, the director of Amnesty International’s French-speaking Belgian section, citing the impact the raids could have on children and on people who had opened their homes to migrants. “It really disseminates fear.”
Officials have said the measures will be targeted at people who have been denied asylum in Belgium, who have ignored orders to leave and who are seen as a threat to public order or national security.

A broad range of critics have said that the law is vague on what constitutes a public threat, citing cases where these terms were used for people who had carried out undeclared work, run a red light or shoplifted, meaning it will be up to individual judges to determine whether private homes can be turned into sites of immigration enforcement.

According to Amnesty International, the judges would not have full investigative powers but instead would be limited on who they could ask for additional information, while the legislation fails to provide a means for people to appeal or challenge any decisions that are made.
“They always say it’s for criminals,” Thibaut said. “We always answer that they already have all the tools to address this problem, because they can do that through the normal justice system.”

Her organisation is among the 20 rights groups that have warned that the law perpetuates the conflation of lack of legal status with delinquency. “The home is inviolable. This constitutional principle should never depend on the administrative status of those who live there,” they said.

The view was echoed at the Brussels-based Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, known as Picum. “This really has nothing to do with people who have committed crimes,” said Chiara Catelli, an advocacy officer. “It’s really about wanting to return people, deporting people, which is an administrative procedure.”

She added: “We’ve all seen the devastating consequences of home raids in the US, where they fuel fear and violence and tear families apart. It’s deeply alarming that an EU member state is now moving in the same direction.”

Catelli noted that similar, hardline measures were already in place in countries such as the Netherlands and Germany. The EU’s recently approved returns regulation, aimed at ramping up deportations across the bloc, includes similar provisions, meaning other member states could soon adopt comparable measures, she said. “We’re really afraid that this is the beginning of something that will become more widespread.”
Thibaut said that measures such as those in Belgium would gradually chip away at the rights of everyone. “It’s the beginning of reducing the state of law and the respect for human rights,” she said.

“This time it is for people without papers; after that, it might be people who are using drugs. That’s the way you slowly, slowly dismantle a society based on human rights, on respect for justice and on separation of powers.”

articles.title: Bird flu fears prompt orders for farmers to keep poultry inside in England and Scotland
articles.summary: Increased risk of devastating strain means restrictions imposed for second year in a row on those keeping birds
body: Poultry and captive birds across England and Scotland must be kept inside for the second year in a row due to an increased risk of a devastating strain of bird flu.

The British government has issued an England-wide avian influenza prevention zone, meaning individuals with 50 or more poultry or captive birds must house them inside. A similar designation was made across the whole of Scotland on Tuesday.
Birdkeepers must also follow enhanced biosecurity measures including reporting changes in egg production and reporting suspected disease immediately to the Animal and Plant Health Agency.
The government said the declaration followed an increased risk and escalating number of confirmations of the highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, in kept and wild birds.
A prevention zone was also declared across all of England, Scotland and Wales in 2025.

The disease has been spreading rapidly since 2014 and has devastated UK wild bird populations since the summer of 2021. It has also spread across an unusually broad range of species around the world, including in four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some south Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females.
Related: Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?
The disease has also been detected in humans, with 11 deaths recorded globally between 1 January and 4 August 2025.
This strain of bird flu causes illness and high death rates in birds, and flu-like symptoms and conjunctivitis in humans who come into close contact with infected animals.
The British government said the current risk to human health from bird flu remained very low.

The government says it does not anticipate an impact on the availability of Christmas turkeys or other seasonal poultry for consumers. The Food Safety Authority said properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, were safe to eat.

The UK chief veterinary officer, Christine Middlemiss, said: “Having avian influenza confirmed in your flock can be devastating. I understand the impact this disease can have on the poultry sector and am extremely grateful for the continued cooperation of the industry.”

articles.title: AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals
articles.summary: 181GW of gas-fired capacity proposed for sites in US and Europe because of delays in connecting to national grids, says report
body: Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying gas power stations on a huge scale to meet their energy demands, research reveals.

Datacentres planned across the US, the UK and mainland Europe have proposals to build fossil fuel plants on-site to create 181GW of gas-fired capacity because of delays to connect to national grids, according to the findings. This is almost four times the total peak electricity demand of Great Britain.

The research by BloombergNEF says this “speed to power” will – if the planned rollout happens – emit about 345m metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year in the US, where 90% of on-site gas-fired power stations are planned. This is equivalent to annual greenhouse gas emissions from about 72.8m fossil fuel cars.

The report was published on Wednesday as global leaders gathered in Turkey for the 31st UN climate summit, where increasing electrification – ideally from clean sources – is a central part of discussions. However, a number of key European leaders, including from France and Germany, will not be at Cop31, instead heading to Dublin where EU leaders will hold their first dedicated AI summit on Friday.

Mark Daly, the head of datacentres and emerging tech at BloombergNEF, said: “The extraordinary economics around AI are making speed to power one of the most important priorities for defining constraints on datacentre developers.

“The climate outcome will depend not only on how much electricity these facilities use, but on how quickly grids can connect them and whether power systems add cleaner generation alongside that demand.”
Related: Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam
By 2035, the electricity demand of AI datacentres was predicted to almost quadruple to 2,354 terawatt-hours – equivalent to 7% of global electricity demand – the report said.
AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cool equipment, and to run facility systems.

Daly said while the developers of the future datacentres claimed their gas-fired power supplies would be temporary while they waited for grid connections, once they were online, the economics could encourage them to continue generating energy, creating a longer-term fossil-fuel lock-in risk.

The report said ensuring new datacentres were connected to the grid was the more sustainable option. Faster grid connections were crucial to limiting emissions impacts and locking in fossil fuel risk, it said.

UK planned datacentres made more than 100 inquiries in 2024-5 to connect to gas as a result of delays in securing access to the electricity grid, according to Future Energy Networks, the representative body for the UK gas networks.

For example, Wapseys Wood, Buckinghamshire and Quest Park, Bedfordshire are seeking to build their own on-site gas-fired power stations because of the long wait to connect to the grid. The datacentres are among the first to be fast-tracked through the government’s nationally significant infrastructure project regime, which allows developers to rapidly deliver major infrastructure, bypassing locally elected planning authorities.

But the use of fossil fuel power generation on site is likely to be repeated by many more UK sites after the chancellor, John Healey, gave the green light for datacentres to build and run temporary on-site fossil fuel power stations while they wait for connections to the grid, as part of a so-called datacentre covenant.

Oliver Hayes, the head of policy and campaigns at Global Action Plan , said: “Private gas power stations for datacentres should be a red line for any government serious about climate action, so it’s shocking to see the chancellor give them his explicit backing.
“No one seriously believes these gas power stations will be temporary – once they’re built, they’ll lock in high emissions for years.”

articles.title: Germany reportedly bans Chinese drones at military bases over security concerns
articles.summary: Western military forces increasingly worried Chinese-made technology ⁠could send ‌sensitive information to Beijing
body: Germany has banned commercially available Chinese-made drones ⁠from its military bases and training grounds due to security concerns, ⁠according to reports.
Western military forces have grown increasingly concerned that Chinese-made technology ⁠could pose a security risk and may be ​used to transmit ‌sensitive information to Beijing.

Germany’s drone ban, effective immediately, follows the US military banning China’s BYD electric vehicles from its Kadena airbase on the Japanese island of Okinawa. Kadena, the biggest US air force base in east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.
Related: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk

The German newspaper Der Spiegel reported that the drones, ‌acquired by military units in recent years with limited bureaucratic oversight, are being withdrawn from service as quickly as possible. The defence ministry was not immediately available for comment.

Local commanders had been allowed to buy the drones under ‌a 2024 strategy that included a “white list” of approved systems, including several made by the ​China-based DJI, the world’s largest drone maker.
As there is no central record of purchases by individual units, the military has to ⁠impose a blanket ban, Der Spiegel reported.
In February, Poland barred Chinese-made vehicles from entering its military facilities over concerns that onboard sensors could be used to collect sensitive data.
The army said Chinese-made vehicles may still be allowed on to secured sites if specified functions are disabled and other safeguards required under each facility’s security rules are in place.

When the US military announced its ban on BYD vehicles entering Kadena airbase, Lt Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force, said: “These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission.”

American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.

In safety advice issued in September, the Dutch government said smart features built into modern vehicles – including microphones, cameras and GPS trackers – could be used by hostile states to spy on people. The warning from the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service did not mention countries or manufacturers by name.

That alert followed reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.

Last week, a group of MEPs urged the European Commission to assess whether BYD cars posed a security threat and should ​be subject to restrictions, such as excluding them from public procurement purchases.
In written questions, 14 ​parliamentarians asked that the EU’s cybersecurity agency assess the level of threat ​and potentially include BYD on a list of high-risk suppliers.
Related: US bans humanoid robots from China, citing ‘unacceptable risks’

François Kalfon, the ⁠French MEP leading the push, wrote in a preamble to the questions that China’s ​2017 national intelligence law required companies to cooperate with the state. “Allowing connected vehicles from third ​countries to access sensitive European infrastructure therefore poses an unacceptable security risk,” he wrote.

In a statement, BYD said no data processed or stored, whether in the cloud or within a vehicle, could be remotely accessed from China, ​and that customers remained in control of their data. “BYD Europe does not make such ​data available to BYD entities or third parties in China.”
In 2018, the US defence department banned the use of smartphones from the Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide, citing security concerns.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: ​How David Walliams tried to silence his accusers
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: ​Our joint investigation with ITV into David Walliams might never have seen the light of day, but his unprecedented attempt to stop publication was rejected by the High Court
body: Good morning. Rumours had been circulating for months. A famous man was attempting to stop the Guardian and ITV News from publishing allegations that he used his power and celebrity to prey on young women and teenagers for sex. Many guessed his identity; stories about his general conduct had occasionally made the news. But these allegations were far more severe and far-reaching.
Yesterday, the Guardian’s investigations team named that man as the comedian, television presenter and children’s author David Walliams.

This investigation is the result of meticulous reporting and interviews with multiple women, some of whom allege that Walliams groomed, pursued and harassed them, two when they were 15. The allegations span nearly two decades. Had the injunction that Walliams’ legal team sought against the Guardian and ITV News been granted, these allegations would never have come to light.
For today’s First Edition, I spoke to the Guardian’s investigations correspondent Maeve McClenaghan, one of the journalists who has been working on this story. First, here are the headlines.

UK news | A US soldier with alleged links to Russia has been arrested as part of an investigation by British counter-terrorism police, working closely with US authorities, the US military and the FBI.

US politics | House Republicans on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, rejecting allegations that the defence secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of the Iran war and other conflicts globally.
US news | Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, have been accused of misleading shareholders in a lawsuit over the Chinese spying scandal engulfing the $4.3tn (£3.2tn) company.
Cop31 | China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian.
Gaza | An independent professor who reviewed the medical records of a prominent Gaza doctor held in an Israeli prison without charge for nearly 23 months has raised serious concerns about his health.

Since making his name in the BBC sketch show Little Britain, David Walliams has become one of Britain’s most successful comedians and authors. He has worked as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent, an actor, and a prolific children’s author. He has cultivated a family-friendly image, particularly through his charity work – after swimming the Channel in 2006, he was voted Britain’s most “inspiring” public figure at the Pride of Britain awards, and in 2017 he received an OBE. Yet rumours persisted about his relationships with women.

In December 2004, Little Britain won the top accolade at the British comedy awards. The show’s host, Jonathan Ross, opened the awards show with a joke referencing its creator. “The comedy awards is 15 years old – 15 years old! And like most 15-year-olds, it’s drunk, it’s unpredictable and it’s probably going home with David Walliams,” he said. (Ross’s lawyers told the Guardian that he did not write this joke himself).

Walliams’ reputation wasn’t entirely unblemished. In November 2022, the Guardian reported on a hot mic incident in which Walliams was recorded making derogatory remarks about contestants on Britain’s Got Talent, referring to them in offensive terms and saying, of one, “she thinks you want to fuck her, but you don’t.” He was dropped from the show, but continued to publish books and appear on television. Then, in December last year, the Telegraph reported that Walliams had been dropped by his publisher, HarperCollins, after allegations that he had “harassed” junior female employees. Walliams denied that he had behaved inappropriately and said he was not informed of any allegations raised against him by HarperCollins.

Maeve and Rachael Healey had been speaking to sources who knew or worked with Walliams since 2022, and started working on a joint investigation with ITV News the following year. In the course of their investigation, they spoke to more than 100 people. One woman said that Walliams pursued her after she attended a fan event when she was 15, and said that by the time she was 17, they were having sex. Another said that Walliams contacted her on Myspace when she was 15, and accused him of later sexually assaulting her. She said that she would sometimes contact Walliams using her school email address.

Another alleges that in 2008, after being invited to a party at Walliams’ home, the wife of a guest pulled her aside and warned: “You’re very young, be careful.” Lawyers for Walliams said he never engaged in grooming young women, and that the allegations of serious criminal conduct are false. More widely, Walliams has denied any wrongdoing, and in a letter to journalists working on this investigation, he said: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 or 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”
“It can take a long time for sources in these type of stories to feel ready to talk on the record,” Maeve tells me. “It can be a long process to build that trust.”
The arguments made by Walliams’ legal team

In May this year, the Guardian and ITV News sent letters to Walliams’ publicist outlining their reporting and requesting a response ahead of publishing. “We heard from his lawyers that Walliams had a reaction to reading those findings, and had attempted to take his own life,” Maeve says. Walliams was hospitalised, and the Guardian and ITV News took advice from an independent psychiatric expert. Walliams’ legal team applied for an injunction to prohibit the Guardian and ITV News from publishing the allegations.

His case hinged on three arguments. First, that publishing these allegations would expose Walliams to a real and immediate risk of serious harm or death (he made a second suicide attempt after absconding from the care of a hospital). Second, that only the court, by issuing an injunction, could protect Walliams’ rights under articles 2 and 3 of the European convention on human rights (the right to life and the right not to be subject to “inhuman or degrading treatment”). And, third, that Walliams’ relationship with his son would be lost or seriously damaged were the allegations published, infringing his right to private and family life.
A celebrity seeking an injunction because they argue that a media story poses a risk to their life is unprecedented, Maeve tells me. “We’d never dealt with this before.”

Both sides agreed to appoint a joint expert witness to assess Walliams’ condition. The expert concluded that Walliams had an “elevated underlying risk of suicide and self-harm,” and that if publication went ahead it would result in a “very substantial increase in the risk of psychiatric deterioration, suicidal ideation and suicidal acts” in Walliams. But the expert’s evidence did not establish that suicide was “an inevitable consequence of publication,” and concluded that psychiatric treatment, support, and continued admission could help reduce this risk.

The Guardian and ITV News’s lawyers argued that granting the injunction would represent a radical, unprincipled expansion of the court’s duties, and that healthcare services were the appropriate bodies to protect Walliams’ rights, not the courts. The judge concluded that while the risk of suicide was genuine and grave, it was not for the court to restrain publication by granting an injunction.

He ruled that the state had assumed responsibility for Walliams’ safety through the psychiatric hospital and mental health services, and that it does not have a duty “to guarantee that suicide will not occur or to eliminate every residual risk”. Walliams was given until 4:30pm on Monday to appeal against the judge’s decision, which he didn’t.

Had Walliams won, the injunction would have applied not only to the Guardian and ITV News’s investigation, but indirectly to the women who came forward and made these allegations. “The idea that the investigation might not get published and, worse, that our sources might then be silenced, was very troubling,” Maeve tells me.

It could also have set a precedent for others to use human rights legislation to block public interest investigations in future. “Obviously we shouldn’t diminish the facts in this particular case, but you can see how a ruling like this would open up an avenue for people to use this argument to shut down investigations,” Maeve says. “And the judge really probed that, and asked, if I rule in favour of this injunction, where will it end?”
The always-affable Jarvis Cocker is on delightful form here recounting his time as a Booker judge, revealing how they picked a winner with no scones thrown. Libby

Not the cheeriest of reads but fascinating and important nonetheless (with some great images to boot), Lana Crowe talks to film storyboard artists about what will be lost if they are replaced by AI. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team
Our senior Washington reporter Chris Stein offers this fascinating insight into GOP thinking post-midterms. Libby

This gallery of photographs from the British music scenes of the 70s and 80s is an absolute banger. The Specials and Sade are among her subjects but my favourite shot is of a group of young female 2 Tone fans, striking a “Madness pose” in their braces, Loakes and Fred Perry shirts. Pure joy. Lucinda

I really enjoyed readers’ suggestions for how to get the buzz back on our high streets, including a pound on residential parcel deliveries and the community cafe in Hastings that launched a local rewards scheme. Libby
Football | Manchester City’s European campaign finally came roaring into life as they thumped Inter 4-1 to record their first Women’s Champions League victory of the season
NFL | Minnesota have acquired Kirk Cousins from Las Vegas for a 2027 third-round pick, clearing the way for rookie Fernando Mendoza to start for the Raiders.

Football | US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino is interested in a move to Manchester United, multiple sources told the Guardian, with those same sources characterising the interest as mutual.

“David Walliams accused of using his celebrity status to prey on young women for sex”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Telegraph has “Walliams faces police investigation”, the Mail says “Teenage girls he targeted in plain sight”, the Mirror also splashes “Hiding in plain sight”, the Sun writes “Named .. & shamed”, and the Express goes with “Accused of preying on girls aged 15”. Metro has “Walliams is unmasked”, and The i Paper has “Walliams accused of preying on girls as young as 15”.
Elsewhere, the Times leads on “HMRC to snoop on £2m homes”, and the FT writes “Anthropic sets sights on $1.4tn value in giant Wall St debut”.
The allegations against David Walliams

Multiple women allege David Walliams abused his power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were young women, an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found. He denies the allegations.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

The modern dating scene is famously bleak – and the apps are the wild west. But maybe we’ve been thinking about human connection all wrong. When Emily’s Bumble date with Steven fizzled, she readied herself for the familiar rush of disappointment, but instead found the unexpected: a beautiful platonic bond blossomed. The experience helped Emily rethink the exhausting pursuit of romantic perfection. “While I didn’t find love … I’ve gained a friend for life in Steven and a shift in perspective: dating apps aren’t the devil.”
Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

articles.title: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment
articles.summary: Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort
body: Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.

The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.

According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.
Related: ‘I made the biggest mistake’: the young Yemeni men lured into the Russian army with empty promises
The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.
In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.

A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.
This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.

Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”
Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.
Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.

The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.

The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).
It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

articles.title: Fresh concerns raised over Gaza doctor held by Israel for 23 months without charge
articles.summary: Independent Israeli professor says Hussam Abu Safiya’s life will be at risk until he receives proper medical treatment
body: An independent professor who reviewed the medical records of a prominent Gaza doctor held in an Israeli prison without charge for nearly 23 months has raised serious concerns about his health.
Hussam Abu Safiya was detained at work on 27 December 2024 and later held in solitary confinement at Rakefet, a notorious underground prison.

During a visit by a lawyer from Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) in the summer, the doctor told of harsh conditions, untreated medical problems and severe food shortages. Witnesses said he had become almost unrecognisable.
Nearly 700 days after his arrest, Israeli authorities have yet to bring any formal charges against Abu Safiya, who is the director of Kamal Adwan hospital in northern Gaza.
He was classified as an “unlawful combatant” along with more than 375 medical workers – a designation Israel has used to justify prolonged detention without trial.

Last month, Israel’s supreme court rejected a petition to release the doctor. Over the weekend, a district court rejected a separate petition to allow Abu Safiya an independent medical examination, despite troubling findings in his medical records that were not adequately investigated, according to Prof Amit Tirosh, an independent Israeli specialist who reviewed a file obtained by PHRI.
In an interview with the Guardian, Tirosh said Abu Safiya’s weight had fallen from 90kg (14st 2lb) in January 2025 to 76kg this May.
“Continuous food deprivation and weight loss, repeated beatings and injuries, with inadequate medical care, can definitely cost Dr Abu Safiya his life,” Tirosh said.
“According to PHRI records, more than 100 prisoners died in Israeli facilities between 2023 and 2025 … a threat to his life unfortunately cannot be ruled out.”
Tirosh identified insufficient investigation of chest pain, delays in treating scabies and a drop in haemoglobin levels that warranted further examination.

“A 14kg weight loss is very alarming, even more so if the cause is unknown,” he added. “More troubling, the medical team was neither surprised nor concerned: one prison physician wrote that his weight loss over a year is ‘a common trend among security prisoners associated to their diet’.
“Haemoglobin dropped between February and July 2026, long after the weight loss, so detention or starvation alone cannot explain it; it coincided with the reported beatings in Rakefet.
“Such blood loss can be life-threatening and requires urgent ER evaluation. Per the records, these urgent problems were not addressed and could endanger his life.”

Medical records documented bruising around one of Abu Safiya’s eyes, dizziness and rib pain in July. He told his lawyers he had been beaten by prison guards but Tirosh said the records did not explain his injuries.

The district court ruling also revealed allegations made by Israeli authorities that Abu Safiya had exaggerated his medical problems, set up organisations from prison, influenced other prisoners and maintained international contacts.
PHRI said the Israeli allegations did not justify denying him an independent medical examination, a right protected by law.
“The bottom line is that a third party should see him and the full medical records,” said Tirosh. ‘‘Refusing an independent examination is never justified.

“To the Israeli prison system authorities I would say that I feel deep shame to be counted with them as a doctor or health provider in Israel. As a system, they betray every medical and ethical principle I stand for.”
The Israeli prison service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Abu Safiya had become the face of health workers struggling to treat patients throughout the war in Gaza before his detention. He is being held indefinitely, along with thousands of other Palestinian civilians, in prisons that Israeli rights groups say have become torture camps.
At the time of his arrest at work, Abu Safiya was wearing a white medical coat that he had refused to wash since his son, Ibrahim, was killed by a drone strike at the hospital entrance that October.
Abu Safiya had helped keep the hospital running through more than 80 days of siege and attacks by Israeli forces amid an intensive military operation in the surrounding refugee camp.

“Fourteen Palestinian doctors, including hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields, remain imprisoned without charge or trial at a time when Gaza’s healthcare system desperately needs them,” said Naji Abbas of PHRI.

A spokesperson for the Israeli prison service (IPS) told the Guardian the allegations are “part of a broader campaign aimed at discrediting the state of Israel” and that the IPS “operates in accordance with the law and under constant judicial oversight”.
Abu Safiya’s family have not been able to communicate with him directly in detention.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Putin ‘lives in a different reality’ as Abu Dhabi talks get under way
articles.summary: Ukrainian president dismisses Moscow’s claims of gains in Donbas region but says first day of trilateral talks were constructive. What we know on day 1,722
body: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has backed Ukraine’s assessment of what is happening on the battlefield and that Vladimir Putin lives in a “different reality”, as American-led trilateral discussions between Ukraine, ⁠Russia and the US got under way in Abu Dhabi. In a post on social media, Zelenskyy said that Russia has claimed at the talks that they occupied half of the Donbas in Ukraine’s east. “This is the problem. Putin lives in a different reality,” the Ukrainian president wrote, adding “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true. What was good is that the American side confirmed the Ukrainian assessment of what is happening on the battlefield.”

Zelenskyy said he was “happy” to see a change in the approach by US mediators at the Abu Dhabi talks. “I see changes. I’m very happy with what I hear. We will see what can be done,” Zelenskyy told a press conference in Copenhagen after being asked about changes in the approach to peace talks made by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.

Zelenskyy described the first day of talks – the first three-sided discussions to be held since February – as constructive and substantive. He said the agenda in Abu Dhabi had included formulating a new security architecture for Europe, an idea raised earlier on Tuesday by Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100% what they want. I think we understand, but nobody ​saw the documents, what the Americans discussed with the Russians,” Zelenskyy said.

In Abu Dhabi, US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war, Andrew Roth and Jennifer Rankin report. Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said, but European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence.

Ukraine’s foreign minister said he ⁠had urged US secretary of state Marco Rubio to accelerate ⁠interceptor ​deliveries as Russia ramps up attacks on energy ⁠infrastructure. Speaking to Reuters after talks ​with Rubio, Andrii Sybiha said he had pressed Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow even as diplomatic efforts to end the war took ‌place in Abu Dhabi. He said Ukraine remained prepared to ​discuss a range of de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure.

Friedrich Merz has signalled he will block the EU’s seven-year budget unless there is a deal on financial aid for Ukraine, triggering accusations of “typical blackmail” from some other European leaders and setting the stage for stormy talks later this month, Jennifer Rankin reports from Brussels. The German chancellor’s intervention has angered leaders in central Europe who are net beneficiaries of EU funds but do not want to take part in an upcoming funding round to support Ukraine’s war effort. “What the chancellor is doing is typical blackmail, and I will not give in to it,” Slovakia’s Russia-friendly prime minister, Robert Fico, told reporters in Bratislava, alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš.

A drone attack sparked a fire at a key Russian port for oil exports, the regional governor announced. “A UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] attack hit the port area of Ust-Luga, causing a fire,” Aleksandr Drozdenko posted on Telegram, referring to one of Russia’s most important western oil hubs that has been repeatedly attacked by Ukraine. Teams were working to extinguish the fire, he added.

Latvia ⁠and Lithuania warned people across several regions to take shelter due ⁠to threats ⁠of ​unidentified drones entering their airspace via neighbouring Russia or Belarus early on Wednesday. Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre said its warning included ⁠the country’s second city of Kaunas, which has ​a population of about ‌300,000 people. As ‌Ukraine attacks Russia’s Baltic Sea oil shipping ports, some of its drones have ​missed their targets and led to security warnings in neighbouring countries. Moscow ⁠has accused Kyiv of using Nato airspace ​as cover ​for attacks, while Kyiv ​says some of its drones have ​been steered off ‌course by Russian ​signal ​jamming. The Nato countries blame Russia for the incidents, saying it ignited the war.

articles.title: Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron file new defamation lawsuit against Candace Owens
articles.summary: Legal battle escalates as far-right US podcaster continues to spread false claims that France’s first lady was born a man
body: Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron have brought a fresh defamation lawsuit against Candace Owens in her home state of Tennessee, in an escalation of a transatlantic legal battle as the far-right US podcaster continues to spread false claims that France’s first lady was born a man.

The Macrons first sued Owens and her media companies in July 2025 in Delaware in response to what the French first couple called “verifiably false and devastating lies” being repeated by Owens on her podcast and on X. According to that lawsuit, those lies included that Brigitte Macron, 73, was born a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her older brother – and committed identity theft to hide a gender transition; that Emmanuel Macron was elected as French president as part of a CIA mind-control program; and that the couple are blood-related relatives committing incest.

A judge ruled that the Macrons’ claim was limited in scope to Owens’s companies registered in Delaware after she successfully argued that the court’s jurisdiction did not extend to her personally as she did not live in that state. The case against her companies remains pending.

Meanwhile, the new lawsuit filed on 4 November in Nashville, Tennessee, where Owens resides, includes 88 counts of defamation, false light and defamation by implication. They are against Owens personally and build on the Macrons’ original demand for punitive damages against the podcaster on the grounds that she has persisted with the false claims.

“Mrs Owens was adamant that Tennessee is where this case belongs because it’s where she lives,” a representative for the Macrons’ legal team said. “With this filing, we are giving her exactly what she has repeatedly demanded.”

The new complaint stated that since the Delaware lawsuit was filed, Owens had “unequivocally doubled down”, publishing further “outlandish, defamatory, and far-fetched fictions” through her eight-part podcast series called “Becoming Brigitte” – along with accompanying posts on X.

The filing also alleges that Owens – who has millions of followers across her podcast and social media channels – has a financial motive in continuing to peddle the false claims. “She has continued to use her podcast to expand her lies about the Macrons, sell merchandise making fun of the Macrons, and collect donations based on her ‘reporting’ on the Macrons,” the complaint says.

The new lawsuit mentions a “Brigitte doll” that Owens holds in her videos, describing it as “a grotesque, alien-like figure” that is reminiscent of the namesake character in the fictional film ET. The doll “caricatures Mrs Macron’s body”, the lawsuit contends, while adding that Owens’s use of the doll confirms “that her campaign against Mrs Macron is driven by animus toward Mrs Macron’s perceived gender identity, gender, and sexuality”.

The French first couple has experienced “relentless bullying on a worldwide scale” as a result, the lawsuit alleges. It says: “Defendant has subjected the Macrons to a campaign of global humiliation, turning their lives into fodder for profit-driven lies. Owens has dissected their appearance, their marriage, their friends, their family, and their personal history – twisting it all into a grotesque narrative designed to inflame and degrade.”
The Macrons are seeking actual, presumed and punitive damages, in addition to a narrowly tailored injunction barring Owens from republishing any defamatory statements.

“To be clear, there is nothing shameful or defamatory about being a man, being transgender, or being gay,” the lawsuit says. “Owens’ statements are defamatory because they accuse the Macrons of lying to France and to the world, for decades, about who Mrs. Macron is – and of committing crimes to conceal that supposed lie.”

The Guardian has contacted Owens for comment. On X, she wrote in part: “The Macrons have indeed filed a NEW set of claims against me. 88 in total, and this time, they want justice over my Brigitte-Doll.
“Those of you who are fans of the show know that Brigitte-Doll has never pursued the limelight. For her to be called ‘grotesque’ by the French couple is hurtful, to say to the least.
“Brigitte-Doll will be making no further statements at this time.”

articles.title: French police raid Ritz hotel in Mohamed Al Fayed sexual abuse investigation
articles.summary: Arrests made after three properties were searched in relation to inquiry into late businessman
body: French police have made arrests after raiding three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, in relation to an investigation into sexual abuse and trafficking by Mohamed Al Fayed.

Several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released, according to the Paris public prosecutor’s office. Another property in Paris and one in Saint-Tropez, both with links to Fayed, were also searched in mid-October.
Several of Fayed’s alleged victims were also interviewed by officers from the organised crime division of the Paris prosecutor’s office.

It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into “allegations of human trafficking committed by an organised group, aggravated pimping committed by an organised group, and rape”.

In an email sent to survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse earlier today, the Metropolitan police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in a coordinated operation with French investigators.

The Paris prosecutor’s office said: “Searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed, and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.”
The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed, it added.

One of the properties that was raided was Castel Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, one of the most exclusive villas on the French Riviera, and where Diana, Princess of Wales, stayed with her sons in the summer of 1997, at the start of her relationship with Fayed’s son, Dodi.

The other was Villa Windsor, a former holiday home of the Fayed family. The property in western Paris was previously the family home of Charles de Gaulle, before he was president of France, and King Edward VIII, after his abdication, and his wife, Wallis Simpson.
A Met spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France last month and were present during the operation.
Campaign groups representing Fayed’s alleged victims called on the Met police to conduct its own searches of the late billionaire’s properties.

Co-chairs of Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors, Jen Mills and Lindsay Mason, said: “We want to see the same thoroughness applied to every property where survivors say they were taken or abused, including here in Britain. The searches in Paris and Saint-Tropez must be the beginning, not the end.”

A spokesperson for No One Above, a collective of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse, said: “The French authorities have put this in the hands of their specialist trafficking unit and their organised crime prosecutors, and are investigating it as trafficking by an organised gang.

“The evidence in this case was never confined to Harrods. For two years, the Met has avoided treating it as what France recognised from the outset: organised trafficking by a network. The National Crime Agency should now take over the investigation.”

Pelham Spong, who says she was trafficked in Paris on Fayed’s orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him, said she was overjoyed by the French police raids. “Survivors deserve actions, not words,” she added.

Last November, she told French investigators from the Central Office for the Repression of Human Trafficking that Fayed, who owned the Ritz hotel in Paris, had forcibly kissed her and offered her a salary of €65,000 a year if she slept with him.

Survivors’ groups say more than 500 women have come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at Harrods, Park Lane, Fulham football club, the Ritz hotel in Paris, and other places owned by Fayed. The Met is investigating 169 victims who have contacted the force directly.

The Ritz Paris told Agence France-Presse news agency that it “does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour” and that it was ready “to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities”.

articles.title: Israeli opposition hurries to seize control as new Knesset is sworn in
articles.summary: Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has mandate to try to form a government – with Netanyahu waiting if he fails
body: Opposition lawmakers have wasted no time after Israel’s new Knesset was sworn in, deploying their majority to seize control of the legislature from Benjamin Netanyhau and his allies.

Although they are still too divided to form a government, the opposition requested a vote for a new speaker, who sets the Knesset’s agenda. Once Netanyahu loyalist Amir Ohana has been replaced, the six opposition parties will be able to work on key legislation even if they fail to broker a coalition.

Priorities include setting up a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks and introducing term limits for Israel’s prime ministers, which could block Netanyahu from taking power again. He has ruled Israel for 19 of the last 30 years.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, now has the presidential mandate to try to form a government. If he fails to broker a deal within six weeks, a second candidate – probably Netanyahu – will get a second chance. Further failure is likely to lead to another election.

Netanyahu responded to the swearing in of the new Knesset on Tuesday with a racist attack on two Palestinian-led opposition parties, whose voters were essential to unseating his coalition, calling their lawmakers “terror supporters”.
Eisenkot denounced his speech as a “delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful” exploitation of a state occasion, that showed the prime minister was unfit for office.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, and Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish-Israeli former police chief who ran on the slate of Islamist Ra’am party, both walked out of Netanyahu’s speech in protest.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the country’s population. Netanyahu put attacks on these voters and their parties at the heart of his campaign, and since polling day has promoted groundless accusations of fraud in their communities in a bid to undermine results.
Election officials say there was no evidence of irregularities that affected the election outcome or compromised its integrity.

A period of prolonged, difficult coalition negotiations or even a new round of elections would extend Netanyahu’s hold on power as caretaker prime minister. But if the fractured opposition can make progress on key legislation, his grip on the state would be weakened.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party submitted a series of bills to the Knesset moments after the swearing in, with backing from other opposition parties.

In addition to term limits and the 7 October inquiry, legislation includes several bills designed to revoke the “judicial overhaul” pursued by Netanyahu, which weakened the power of Israel’s judiciary and the attorney general.
Ohana has tabled the vote on a new speaker to replace him for next Tuesday, the latest date possible. The opposition have also nominated candidates to take over key defence and finance committees.

Eisenkot has admitted the path to power is “extraordinarily complex”, because of incompatible election promises made by different parties, but described ousting Netanyahu as a national emergency that could require breaking promises.
At the swearing-in ceremony, the president, Isaac Herzog, warned lawmakers they should do everything in their power to avoid a second election.

“Reach out a hand for compromise, even between ⁠rivals … Look upon one another with generosity. There is much work to be done here, and it requires the ability and experience found in every part of this House.“

articles.title: Activist wins 10-year fight against homophobic Trinidad and Tobago laws
articles.summary: Jason Jones welcomes decision by privy council in London to overturn 2025 ruling that outlawed anal sex
body: A gay man has won a historic 10-year battle against Trinidad and Tobago’s homophobic laws with a landmark UK appeals court ruling that could help overturn similar anti-gay laws in other Caribbean countries.

The privy council, based in London, overturned a 2025 decision by Trinidad and Tobago’s court of appeal that recriminalised consensual anal sex, seven years after the Trinidadian activist Jason Jones secured a high court judgment declaring the country’s colonial-era “buggery” laws unconstitutional.

Delivering the ruling, the privy council judge Lord Sales said: “The ability to form a deep connection with another person through an intimate and loving relationship is a vital interest for all human beings.”

The privy council is the final court of appeal for Trinidad and Tobago and several other Commonwealth countries, giving the ruling potentially far-reaching significance for other Caribbean jurisdictions where similar laws remain in force.
“This judgment will have a domino effect across every country that has the privy council as its supreme court. It will change many millions of people’s lives,” Jones said in a statement.
“I’m looking forward to going home, switching off everything and living with this moment for a while.”

In an interview after Tuesday’s hearing, he added: “We may not see the benefits of this for 50 years. What a judgment says in a courtroom and what happens in your home and workplace are two entirely different things.
“I don’t focus on changing hearts and minds. I have done this for my community, for our hearts and minds, so that we can stand proudly and at least say we are not criminals.”

The LGBTQ+ rights activist Peter Tatchell, who was also at the courthouse, said: “There will certainly be LGBT people and human rights defenders in at least a dozen countries who will now use this privy council judgment to push for decriminalisation in their home countries. It sets an absolute gold standard for decriminalisation.”

Jones’s lawyer, Caroline Edwards, hailed Tuesday’s unanimous victory as “an emphatic victory for Jason, for all gay men and women in Trinidad and Tobago and for all people who believe in the fundamental rights of everyone”.

Reflecting on the case’s long journey, she said: “All judges who heard the case in Trinidad and Tobago were unanimous that the 1986 legislation was not justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for rights and freedoms, and all the privy council judges agreed.”

Jones has been fighting the “buggery law”, introduced in 1925 under British colonial rule, since 2016, arguing that it violated his constitutional rights. His case hinged on whether the provisions criminalising consensual anal sex were protected by the “savings clause”, which shields certain older laws inherited from the UK at independence from being struck down as unconstitutional.

In a historic 2018 victory, the high court judge Devindra Rampersad ruled that the provisions criminalising consensual anal sex were unconstitutional. But the government appealed and last year won a ruling reversing that decision after the court of appeal found the provisions were protected by the savings clause.

Tuesday’s privy council decision backed Rampersad’s original ruling, with all five judges finding that parliament’s 1986 Sexual Offences Act amounted to new legislation rather than merely a continuation of colonial-era laws and therefore could not be protected from constitutional challenge by the savings clause.

The privy council also upheld Rampersad’s remedy that makes anal sex legal between consenting adults of any gender over the age of 16. It also decriminalises same-sex intimacy, referred to in the archaic 1925 act as “gross indecency”.

Jones’s court case is the latest significant victory for LGBTQ+ rights in the Caribbean. It follows a landmark ruling in St Lucia last year, when the Eastern Caribbean supreme court struck down colonial-era laws criminalising consensual gay sex.
Jeshua Bardoo, a lawyer and founder of Equal Rights, Access and Opportunities St Vincent and the Grenadines, described Tuesday’s decision as a “historic moment for LGBTQ+ rights”.

“Unfortunately, in my country, SVG, a high court judge upheld these laws as constitutional in 2024. I believe that this decision will be very persuasive to the case currently under way or future litigation in SVG, as privy council decisions are usually binding on lower courts,” he said.

Joel Simpson, the founder of the Society Against Sexual Orientation Discrimination, a Guyanese LGBTQ rights organisation, described the ruling as a “monumental victory for LGBTQIA+ people in Trinidad and Tobago and across the Caribbean”.

“This ruling is another powerful sign of the growing momentum across the Caribbean to leave behind outdated colonial-era laws that criminalise people simply because of who they are and who they love,” he said.

Téa Braun, the chief executive of the Human Dignity Trust, said there was hope the case signalled a continuing regional trend of tackling “antiquated laws” that “violate the human rights of LGBTQ+ people”.

“This issue continues to be litigated in domestic courts across the region, and we hope the trend – which began with a judgment in Belize in 2016 and was followed by Antigua, Barbados, St Kitts, Dominica and St Lucia – will continue,” she said.
In Trinidad and Tobago, Pride TT welcomed the ruling as a “significant moment in Trinidad and Tobago’s journey towards equality”, but said it did not mean the struggle for LGBTQ+ people was over.
“We must acknowledge that the removal of these discriminatory provisions does not mean that all the challenges facing LGBTQIA+ people have suddenly disappeared,” it said.
“Discrimination, stigma, exclusion and unequal treatment remain realities in many aspects of everyday life, including employment, education, housing, healthcare and access to public services.”

Asked whether this would make Jones, who has lived in London for several decades, feel comfortable living in Trinidad again, he said no. “The thing about liberation movements is every time you move the needle forward, you get the pushback. I got a lot of pushback from the queer community [in Trinidad], saying: ‘Don’t stir the pot.’ But you have to. I’m not afraid of pushback.”
